item.title: Reconstruction of daily snow depth at 0.25° resolution over the arid regions of Central Asia from 1980 to 2023 using machine learning
item.dc:title: Reconstruction of daily snow depth at 0.25° resolution over the arid regions of Central Asia from 1980 to 2023 using machine learning
item.dc:creator: Liancheng Zhang Guli Jiapaer Tao Yu Jie Bai Xiapeng Jiang Hongwu Liang Pingping Feng Tongwei Ju Philippe De Maeyer Tim Van de Voorde a Xinjiang Uygur Autonomous Region Climate Center (Xinjiang Environment and Resources Remote Sensing Center), Urumqi, Chinab State Key Laboratory of Ecological Safety and Sustainable Development in Arid Lands, Xinjiang Institute of Ecology and Geography, Chinese Academy of Sciences, Urumqi, Chinac University of Chinese Academy of Sciences, Beijing, Chinad Sino-Belgian Joint Laboratory for Geo-Information, Urumqi, Chinae Key Laboratory of GIS & RS Application, Xinjiang Uygur Autonomous Region, Urumqi, Chinaf Department of Geography, Ghent University, Ghent, Belgiumg Sino-Belgian Joint Laboratory for Geo-Information, Ghent, BelgiumLiancheng Zhang received his Ph.D. in Cartography and Geographic Information Systems from the Xinjiang Institute of Ecology and Geography, Chinese Academy of Sciences in 2026. He is currently a Senior Engineer at the Xinjiang Climate Center. His research primarily focuses on climate change and ecological remote sensing in arid regions. Guli Jiapaer received her Ph.D. in Cartography and Geographic Information Systems in 2008 from the Graduate University of the Chinese Academy of Sciences and the Xinjiang Institute of Ecology and Geography, Chinese Academy of Sciences. She is currently a Professor and Doctoral Supervisor at the Xinjiang Institute of Ecology and Geography, Chinese Academy of Sciences. Her research focuses on quantitative remote sensing retrieval of surface parameters in arid regions and the analysis of arid land surface environmental changes and their driving forces. Tao Yu received his Ph.D. in Cartography and Geographic Information Systems from the Xinjiang Institute of Ecology and Geography, Chinese Academy of Sciences in 2024. He is currently a Postdoctoral Researcher at the Xinjiang Institute of Ecology and Geography, Chinese Academy of Sciences. His research interests include vegetation carbon cycle modeling and eco-hydrology. Jie Bai received her Ph.D. in Cartography and Geographic Information Systems from the Xinjiang Institute of Ecology and Geography, Chinese Academy of Sciences in 2010. She is currently a Professor at the Xinjiang Institute of Ecology and Geography, Chinese Academy of Sciences. Her research focuses on agricultural remote sensing and agricultural water consumption. Xiapeng Jiang received his M.E. degree in Geo-informatics and smart city from Shenzhen University (China) in 2022. He is currently pursuing his Ph.D. degree in Geography at the 3D data acquisition of Ghent University (Belgium). His research focuses on multi-scale modeling of potential waterbird habitats driven by multi-source data fusion under machine learning. Hongwu Liang received his Master’s degree in Cartography and Geographic Information Systems from Xinjiang Normal University in 2023. He is currently pursuing a Ph.D. degree at the Xinjiang Institute of Ecology and Geography, Chinese Academy of Sciences. His research has primarily focused on vegetation responses to water stress in arid regions. Pingping Feng received her Master’s degree in Physical Geography from Xinjiang University in 2024. She is currently pursuing a Ph.D. degree at the Xinjiang Institute of Ecology and Geography, Chinese Academy of Sciences. Her research focuses on grassland degradation, desertification, and soil salinization. Tongwei Ju received her Bachelor’s degree in Geographical Science from Qufu Normal University in 2023. She is currently pursuing a Ph.D. degree at the Xinjiang Institute of Ecology and Geography, Chinese Academy of Sciences. Her research has focused on ecological remote sensing, UAV data analysis, and spatial data mining. Philippe De Maeyer received his Master’s degree in Geography from Ghent University, Belgium, in 1976. He is currently an emeritus Senior Full Professor at Ghent University. His research interests include GI capture, modeling and cartography for World Heritage applications.Tim Van de Voorde received the Ph.D. degree in Geography from Vrije Universiteit Brussel (VUB), Brussels, Belgium in 2011. Since 1998, he has been with the Cartography and GIS Research Group, VUB, as a Research Associate. In 2017, he joined the Geography Department, Ghent University, Ghent, Belgium, where he is currently a Professor of remote sensing. His research interests include environmental Earth observation, ecosystem services, and GeoAI.

item.title: Driving forces of contemporary wildfire severity in the American Southwest: a remote sensing and machine learning case study in Arizona, USA
item.dc:title: Driving forces of contemporary wildfire severity in the American Southwest: a remote sensing and machine learning case study in Arizona, USA
item.dc:creator: Helen M. Poulos Sarah Hardy Jenna Otaola Andrew M. Barton a Department of Earth and Environmental Sciences and Bailey College of the Environment, Wesleyan University, Middletown, CT, USAb Department of Biology, University of Maine at Farmington, Farmington, ME, USAc Department of Mathematics, University of Maine at Farmington, Farmington, ME, USAHelen M. Poulos teaches environmental science and environmental studies at Wesleyan University. Her research investigates the impacts and responses of plants to climate change and increasing wildfire activity in the Anthropocene. Over the last two decades, she has studied the shifting dynamics and plant community ecology of high-elevation biodiversity hotspots in the US-Mexico Borderlands. Her research integrates diverse methodologies and analytical approaches including field measurements, dendrochronology, ecophysiology, multivariate statistical modeling, geographic information systems, and remote sensing to quantify how plant abundances and distributions are being impacted by contemporary global environmental change. Sarah Hardy is Professor Emerita of Mathematics at the University of Maine at Farmington. Sarah has 30 years of data analysis and visualization experience in the R programming language. She is an expert in multivariate data mining and statistical modelling methodology including Random Forests. Jenna Otaola is an environmental scientist at GEI consultants in Glastonbury, Connecticut and a graduate of Wesleyan University’s Earth and Environmental Sciences Program. She provides Geotechnical, Environmental, Water Resources management consulting services to a wide range of private firms and public organizations. Andrew M. Barton is a forest and fire ecologist and science writer. He uses field demography, dendrochronology, plant physiology, and remote sensing to investigate the responses of forests and endangered plants to changing climate and wildfire in the Southwest, northern Mexico, and Maine. He received his Ph.D. from the University of Michigan and is currently a professor of biology at the University of Maine at Farmington.
